operationalization: For continental islands, model mammal taxonomic or phylogenetic similarity to the nearest mainland against channel depth while controlling for distance, island area and climate. A persistent negative depth effect confirms the claim; no effect or the opposite refutes it.

candidate_datasets.name: Global Biodiversity Information Facility
candidate_datasets.role: georeferenced mammal occurrences on islands and mainlands

candidate_datasets.name: GEBCO
candidate_datasets.role: global bathymetry for minimum and historical channel-depth estimates

obstacles: Present bathymetry may differ from channels exposed at past low sea levels.
Introductions and incomplete island inventories can distort affinity.
rationale: The variables have direct modern measures and suitable global databases. Historical connectivity and correlated geography limit causal discrimination, but stratified sensitivity analyses are feasible.

operationalization: For native island endemics, compare phylogenetic distance to biotas of the nearest continent and other islands with distance to environmentally most similar remote regions. The claim is supported if nearest-source affinity predominates across clades and archipelagos.

candidate_datasets.name: Global Biodiversity Information Facility
candidate_datasets.role: species distributions and island occurrence records

candidate_datasets.name: WorldClim
candidate_datasets.role: climate similarity among islands and potential source regions

obstacles: Endemic and native status is unevenly curated.
Some source populations are extinct or unsampled.
rationale: Biogeographic affinity, proximity and environmental similarity are measurable with open global data. Coverage is broad but not complete for poorly known taxa, and extinction can hide the true source.

operationalization: Measure whether endemic species from different islands in each archipelago are phylogenetically closer to one another than to species elsewhere, using clade-specific trees and null models. Consistent within-archipelago clustering confirms the empirical prediction.

candidate_datasets.name: GenBank
candidate_datasets.role: sequence data for focused archipelago phylogenies

obstacles: Polyphyletic colonization can occur within an archipelago.
Sequence coverage is sparse for many endemic invertebrates and plants.
rationale: The closeness prediction is explicit and can be tested with phylogenetic clustering. Existing coverage is strong for well-studied archipelagos but insufficient for the full taxonomic scope.

operationalization: Compare taxonomic and phylogenetic distance from established introduced species to recipient native floras and faunas against matched non-naturalized introductions or source pools. A predominance of distant naturalizers, including genera absent natively, supports the claim.

candidate_datasets.name: Global Register of Introduced and Invasive Species
candidate_datasets.role: country-level introduced and invasive species records

candidate_datasets.name: Open Tree of Life
candidate_datasets.role: phylogenetic distances to recipient native species

obstacles: Introduction effort and propagule pressure confound establishment.
Global naturalization data are much stronger for plants than animals.
rationale: Relatedness and establishment are measurable, and substantial open plant data exist. The comparison needed to infer that close relatives are equally fitted is poorly observed, so only the general pattern is currently resolvable.

operationalization: Infer source regions for insular, montane, aquatic, marsh and cave lineages from dated phylogenies and ancestral ranges, then compare inferred sources with quantified dispersal accessibility and test for post-colonization trait shifts. Concordant accessible sources and derived local adaptations support the claim.

candidate_datasets.name: GenBank
candidate_datasets.role: sequence data for phylogeographic source inference

obstacles: Accessibility is lineage- and time-dependent and requires substantial interpretation.
Extinction and range shifts can erase source populations.
Adaptation to the new home is not directly recorded for most lineages.
rationale: Modern phylogeography can test many examples, but no harmonized dataset spans all listed environments and taxa. Historical-source inference and evidence of subsequent adaptation remain confounded and specialist-intensive.

operationalization: Across pairs of regions, quantify counts of close phylogenetic replacements and test whether those counts predict shared species after controlling for area, distance and sampling. A reliably positive association supports the prediction; region pairs with many allied forms but no shared species refute its universal wording.

candidate_datasets.name: Global Biodiversity Information Facility
candidate_datasets.role: regional species assemblages and shared-species counts

candidate_datasets.name: Open Tree of Life
candidate_datasets.role: identification of allied or representative species

obstacles: Species concepts and doubtful forms vary among taxonomic authorities.
Unequal inventory effort creates false absences.
rationale: The universal prediction has a clear counterexample criterion and broad occurrence and phylogenetic data exist. Taxonomic uncertainty and sampling incompleteness reduce confidence but can be modeled.

operationalization: Replace the obsolete lower-to-higher scale with prespecified traits such as body size, propagule size, structural complexity or clade age, and model geographic range size across species. The claim is supported only for operationalizations showing a robust negative association with range.
obstacles: The 'scale of nature' has no accepted measurable ordering.
Occurrence density and taxonomy differ sharply among groups.
rationale: Range size is measurable, but the explanatory variable requires a substantial and contestable modern reinterpretation. Existing data can test trait-specific proxies, not Darwin's ordering as stated.

operationalization: For pairs of living and fossil taxa, regress geographic and temporal separation on phylogenetic distance while accounting for sampling and clade. A general increase in separation with evolutionary distance supports the prediction.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: fossil occurrences with ages and locations

obstacles: Spatial autocorrelation and uneven fossil sampling can create the pattern.
Fossil placements and ages are uncertain.
rationale: All principal quantities have standard definitions and public data. A broad multi-clade analysis is feasible, though the fossil record makes full-scope estimates biased.

operationalization: Quantify hierarchical phylogenetic structure and compare diversification models with descent, trait divergence and extinction against models lacking those processes. Support requires nested monophyletic clusters and model evidence that divergence plus lineage loss generated observed gaps.

candidate_datasets.name: GenBank
candidate_datasets.role: independent sequence characters for phylogenetic reconstruction

obstacles: Nestedness partly follows from tree-based representation.
Extinction histories are incomplete and alternative diversification processes can yield similar patterns.
rationale: Nested descent is exceptionally well documented, but attributing the hierarchy specifically to divergence plus extermination is model-dependent. Phylogenies used to test the claim can introduce circularity unless built from independent characters.

operationalization: Compare independently inferred molecular phylogenetic distances with historical and modern classifications and organismal similarity matrices. Stronger agreement with common descent than with non-genealogical similarity schemes supports the empirical content, but cannot establish the philosophical phrase 'only known cause.'
obstacles: The 'Natural System' and 'something more' are partly conceptual.
Modern classifications often already incorporate phylogenies, creating circularity.
rationale: The correspondence between classification and descent is testable using independent evidence. The uniqueness and conceptual identity claims cannot be fully adjudicated by datasets.

operationalization: Across annotated morphological characters, test whether characters with weaker ecological or functional association have lower evolutionary transition rates and greater congruence with independently inferred molecular trees. The predicted joint pattern supports the claim.

candidate_datasets.name: TreeBASE
candidate_datasets.role: phylogenetic trees and underlying character matrices

obstacles: Functional involvement is rarely coded consistently.
Published matrices select characters for informativeness and are not an unbiased sample.
rationale: Constancy and phylogenetic utility can be quantified, but adaptation involvement requires expert annotation. Existing data support focused clades rather than animals and plants generally.

operationalization: Measure variation among taxonomic authorities and through time in rank assignments for equivalent clades, and test whether added species richness predicts rank elevation independent of clade age or divergence. High instability supports arbitrariness, though no dataset can define how much instability counts as 'almost arbitrary.'

candidate_datasets.name: GBIF Backbone Taxonomy
candidate_datasets.role: alternative global rank assignments and synonymy

obstacles: Arbitrariness is a normative concept without a unique threshold.
Historical taxonomic versions are not uniformly digitized.
rationale: Rank instability and determinants are empirically measurable. The central judgment that ranks are arbitrary remains partly conceptual, and modern taxonomic practice differs from Darwin's period.

operationalization: For sister clades of equal genealogical depth, compare morphological or molecular disparity and assigned Linnaean ranks. Frequent large disparity and rank differences among equally related branches support the claim.

candidate_datasets.name: Open Tree of Life
candidate_datasets.role: identification of equally related sister clades

obstacles: Amount of modification has multiple legitimate metrics.
Morphological matrices are taxonomically selective.
rationale: Sister relationships, phenotypic disparity and rank are measurable with existing data. Different modification metrics limit universality but not the core prediction.

operationalization: Within domestic breeds and well-sampled wild varieties, test whether recognized sub-varieties form genetically nested descent clusters and whether phenotypic distance increases along that hierarchy. Congruent genetic nesting supports descent with modification.

candidate_datasets.name: European Variation Archive
candidate_datasets.role: public genetic variation data for domestic and wild populations

candidate_datasets.name: Dryad
candidate_datasets.role: published breed and population genotype-phenotype datasets

obstacles: Variety and sub-variety labels are inconsistently defined.
Hybridization and repeated artificial selection blur nested descent.
No harmonized dataset spans domestic and natural varieties.
rationale: Genomics can resolve the claim in selected breeds and species. Data and labels are fragmented, so the full stated scope would require extensive compilation.

operationalization: For shared morphological characters across ecologically divergent species, compare their distribution with independent molecular phylogenies and models of common inheritance versus convergence. Broad phylogenetic congruence despite habitat divergence supports inheritance and classificatory value.
obstacles: The assertion 'only' is difficult to establish because convergence is always possible.
Trifling and rudimentary characters are inconsistently annotated.
rationale: Independent molecular evidence can test common inheritance for many specific characters. Public morphology data are selective, and universal exclusion of convergence is not possible.

operationalization: Identify distantly related lineages independently occupying similar environments and test for convergent external morphology, then compare morphology-based grouping with independent molecular phylogeny. Convergence plus reduced classification accuracy supports the claim.
obstacles: Environmental similarity and external resemblance require prespecified metrics.
Published examples may be enriched for known convergence.
rationale: Convergent evolution has clear measurable predictions and can be evaluated independently of morphology. Broad cross-taxon coverage is incomplete, but many replicated clade-level tests are possible now.

operationalization: Define dominance by abundance, range and species richness, then use fossil time series to test whether dominant clades preferentially diversify while smaller clades decline, and whether this process predicts concentration into few high-level groups. Support requires temporal replacement rather than merely present-day imbalance.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: clade diversity, occurrence and extinction through time

obstacles: Dominant and feeble are ambiguous and potentially circular.
Fossil sampling strongly affects apparent diversity and replacement.
Few high ranks may partly reflect classification conventions.
rationale: Parts of the proposed expansion-and-replacement mechanism are testable in well-sampled fossil groups. Explaining the entire hierarchy of life from that mechanism is underdetermined and data coverage is uneven.

operationalization: Define aberrance as high phylogenetic isolation, then test whether isolated extant clades have low extant richness, high pairwise disparity, and fossil evidence of formerly greater diversity. Joint evidence supports their interpretation as extinction relicts.
obstacles: Aberrant is a historical qualitative category.
Missing fossils can make a genuinely old sparse clade appear always species-poor.
rationale: A modern phylogenetic-isolation operationalization permits a strong partial test. Fossil completeness is inadequate to establish severe extinction for all isolated groups.

operationalization: Code claimed cross-group morphological affinities and test whether each character maps broadly near the common ancestor of both groups rather than uniquely linking particular terminal species. A predominance of ancestral, broadly distributed characters supports the claim.
obstacles: Affinity, general and special need expert coding.
Available matrices are not a representative sample of asserted cross-group affinities.
rationale: Ancestral character reconstruction can test specific examples. The qualitative categories and lack of a comprehensive affinity dataset prevent a general resolution.

operationalization: Use dated phylogenies and fossils to identify stem groups with intermediate character combinations and estimate whether lineage extinction enlarged morphological gaps between surviving crown groups. Discovery and temporal loss of intermediates, especially on the bird stem, supports the claim.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: occurrences and ages of extinct connecting forms

candidate_datasets.name: Open Tree of Life
candidate_datasets.role: relationships among living and sampled extinct groups

obstacles: The fossil record cannot reveal forms lost without preservation.
Morphological gaps depend on character choice and surviving sampling.
rationale: Numerous fossils and phylogenetic methods permit direct tests for several major gaps. The assertion about all class-level intervals cannot be completely resolved because extinct diversity is incompletely sampled.

operationalization: For homologous serial elements across sampled classes, code topology of anatomical connections and test whether order is invariant despite variation in element size and shape. Any well-supported transposition refutes the universal claim.
obstacles: Homology assignments can be disputed after fusion or loss.
No public dataset exhaustively codes connection order across all cited classes.
rationale: The invariant-order statement is precise and readily falsifiable. Existing imaging and character data test many examples but do not cover the universal taxonomic scope.

operationalization: Reconstruct ancestral anatomical patterns from independent phylogenies and comparative morphology, then test whether homologous organs are parsimoniously derived by successive modifications without topological transposition. Concordant ancestral patterns and graded transformations support the account.
obstacles: Ancestral states are inferred rather than directly observed.
Gradual and selection-driven modification can be difficult to separate from other evolutionary mechanisms.
rationale: Common ancestry of homologous patterns and transformation sequences are strongly testable with independent molecular and fossil data. Attribution of every step to natural selection is less discriminating, but the central historical inference is resolvable.

operationalization: Map serial-element counts, developmental gene expression and morphology onto vertebrate, arthropod and flowering-plant phylogenies to infer whether their ancestors had repeated similar modules subsequently differentiated. Reconstructed high repetition at the relevant ancestors supports the claim.

candidate_datasets.name: Gene Expression Omnibus
candidate_datasets.role: developmental expression evidence for shared serial identity

obstacles: Deep ancestral states are highly model-dependent.
Comparable developmental data are sparse across all three lineages.
The historical term articulata combines lineages no longer treated as one group.
rationale: Modularity and ancestral repetition can be tested in particular systems. Deep-time coverage and cross-lineage harmonization are insufficient to resolve the complete mechanism.

operationalization: Use stage-matched embryo images or landmark data to compare within-class interspecific morphological distances during development with adult distances and test association with ecological conditions. Lower embryonic than adult disparity and weak embryo-environment association support the claim.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: comparative embryonic and adult morphology where available

obstacles: Developmental stages are difficult to align across species.
Open embryo imaging is concentrated in model organisms rather than whole classes.
rationale: Morphological similarity through ontogeny has a clear quantitative test. Existing public data cover selected vertebrates and insects, not the stated breadth.

operationalization: Define adaptation as survival or performance relative to feasible alternatives, then compare active larval and adult stage-specific performance and phylogenetic disparity in species with free-living larvae. Equivalent standardized performance and occasional greater larval disparity support the measurable portion.

candidate_datasets.name: Dryad
candidate_datasets.role: published larval performance and morphology datasets

candidate_datasets.name: Global Biodiversity Information Facility
candidate_datasets.role: distributions and environmental contexts of species with active larvae

obstacles: 'Perfectly adapted' has no absolute measurable scale.
Stage-specific fitness data are scattered and environmentally contingent.
Survivorship creates strong ascertainment bias.
rationale: Comparative performance and disparity are testable proxies, but perfection is not operationally defined. Existing public data are narrow and scattered, allowing only restricted tests.

operationalization: For multiple breeds of dogs, horses and pigeons, quantify standardized body-shape disparity at matched juvenile and adult ages and test whether between-breed disparity increases with age. Developmental timing of breed-associated alleles can separately test corresponding-age expression.

candidate_datasets.name: European Variation Archive
candidate_datasets.role: breed genetic variants and public genotype studies

candidate_datasets.name: Dryad
candidate_datasets.role: published morphometric and developmental breed datasets

obstacles: Longitudinal, age-matched morphology is not harmonized across the three domestic species.
Breed standards and management alter growth trajectories.
rationale: The age-by-breed disparity prediction is direct and strongly discriminating. Data exist for subsets and individual studies, but a full three-species test requires substantial compilation.

operationalization: Quantify embryonic character similarity among animal groups and test whether it predicts independently inferred molecular common ancestry and improves classification relative to adult convergence-prone characters. Agreement supports embryonic structure as evidence of descent.
obstacles: Embryonic datasets are strongly biased toward model species.
Developmental similarity may reflect constraint as well as ancestry.
rationale: Independent genomic phylogenies make the central evidential relation testable. The stronger claim that embryos directly preserve progenitor structure and are the most valuable characters is only partly discriminated.

operationalization: For fossil stem taxa with credible descendant crown groups, compare adult fossil morphology with stage-matched ontogenetic morphologies of living descendants and appropriate adult controls. Excess resemblance to earlier developmental stages supports the prediction.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: ages and placements of candidate fossil ancestors or stem taxa

obstacles: Direct ancestor-descendant relationships are rarely identifiable.
Adult fossils and embryos differ in size, function and preservation.
The oldest relevant forms are sparsely preserved.
rationale: The resemblance prediction can be tested in selected well-sampled lineages. Deep-time preservation and uncertain ancestry make a general test inadequate and potentially confounded by shared primitive traits.

operationalization: Across related species, estimate developmental onset of derived phenotypic and gene-expression differences and test whether onset timing is conserved between parents and offspring and biased toward later stages. The joint late-onset and corresponding-age pattern supports the mechanism.
obstacles: Comparable developmental staging across species is difficult.
Cause, first phenotypic appearance and inheritance timing are distinct variables.
Public time series cover few clades.
rationale: Modern developmental time series provide a direct test for selected species. Current coverage is too narrow to explain the leading facts of embryology across animals generally.

operationalization: Define rudimentary organs by reduced size or function relative to homologues and estimate their prevalence across a stratified sample of animal and plant taxa. A high prevalence across major clades supports 'extremely common'; consistently low prevalence refutes it.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoBank
candidate_datasets.role: morphological matrices containing reduced or absent structures

candidate_datasets.name: Phenoscape Knowledgebase
candidate_datasets.role: computable vertebrate phenotype and anatomy annotations

obstacles: Uselessness is often unknown and reduction thresholds are subjective.
Databases do not systematically record vestigial organs or true absences.
Published morphology overrepresents unusual structures.
rationale: Prevalence is in principle straightforward, but rudimentary status requires interpretation. Existing databases contain many examples without representative sampling across nature.

operationalization: Compare within-species variance of rudimentary structures with homologous functional structures, and compare reduction levels among sister species. Elevated variance and divergent reduction support the empirical claim; neutrality tests can assess the proposed release from selection.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: individual-level anatomical scans for measurable rudiments

obstacles: Individual-level samples for vestigial organs are rare.
Measurement error rises as structures become very small.
Relaxed selection is not the only cause of high variation.
rationale: The variance comparison is clear, but suitable open samples exist only for scattered structures and taxa. The causal selection explanation has moderate rather than decisive discrimination.

operationalization: Measure each rudiment relative to homologous adjoining structures across embryonic and adult stages and record transient rudiments that disappear. Any robust case with a smaller relative embryonic rudiment refutes the universal rule.
obstacles: Ontogenetic series of known rudiments are sparse outside model organisms.
Choice of adjoining-part denominator can change relative-size conclusions.
rationale: The universal quantitative prediction is highly falsifiable. Public developmental data can test examples but lack representative coverage of animal and plant rudiments.

operationalization: Across replicated losses such as cave eyes and island-bird wings, compare genomic and phenotypic signatures predicted by relaxed selection, direct selection for reduction and inherited effects of use. Estimate which process explains most reductions and whether developmental timing predicts embryonic retention.

candidate_datasets.name: GenBank
candidate_datasets.role: sequences from lineages with reduced organs

candidate_datasets.name: European Nucleotide Archive
candidate_datasets.role: genomic data for relaxed-selection and selection tests

obstacles: Darwin's inherited disuse differs from modern relaxed selection and is hard to map unambiguously.
Selection, drift and developmental pleiotropy produce overlapping signatures.
The claim that disuse is the main agency requires representative global cases.
rationale: Modern comparative genomics can discriminate mechanisms in selected repeated losses. The Lamarckian component and global predominance claim are poorly operationalized and inadequately sampled.

operationalization: Use independent genomic characters to test whether sampled members of each recognized class form connected genealogical trees and whether fossils, rudiments, homologues and embryos are congruent with those trees. Persistent independent evidence for separate origins within a class would refute the claim.

candidate_datasets.name: GenBank
candidate_datasets.role: genome and sequence evidence across classes

obstacles: Classes are human-defined and their circumscriptions change.
Universal common descent is inferred rather than experimentally observed.
rationale: Multiple large independent molecular datasets make common descent within classes strongly testable. Sampling is broad enough for the claim's core, although extinct and microbial diversity remain incomplete.

operationalization: Test whether animal and plant genomes support no more than five independent root lineages within each kingdom, using conserved genes, rare genomic changes and nested homology. Evidence requiring more than five unrelated origins would refute the bound.

candidate_datasets.name: GenBank
candidate_datasets.role: broad genomic sampling of animals and plants

candidate_datasets.name: UniProt
candidate_datasets.role: conserved protein homologies across deep lineages

obstacles: Horizontal gene transfer and deep saturation complicate root inference.
The exact identity of a primordial progenitor is not directly observable.
rationale: The numerical upper bound has clear genomic consequences, and public molecular coverage is extensive. Deep-root reconstruction is difficult, but many independent shared derived features give substantial discriminating power.

operationalization: Compare cellular organization, core biochemical components, conserved growth and reproduction machinery, and toxicant targets across a taxonomically stratified sample of life. Shared core features support the claim; major lineages lacking them would delimit or refute its universal wording.

candidate_datasets.name: UniProt
candidate_datasets.role: cross-organism protein functions and conserved biochemical machinery

candidate_datasets.name: PubChem
candidate_datasets.role: bioassay and toxicant-target data across organisms

obstacles: Germinal vesicles do not apply literally to all living organisms.
Viruses complicate the boundary of living things.
rationale: The shared cellular and biochemical features map directly to abundant public comparative data. Some nineteenth-century terms require reinterpretation, but the core generalization is readily assessed.

operationalization: Test universal common ancestry against multiple-origin models using conserved molecular machinery, near-universal genes, the genetic code and rare shared features while accounting for horizontal transfer. Strong likelihood or model-selection support for one connected ancestry supports the claim.

candidate_datasets.name: UniProt
candidate_datasets.role: universal protein homologies and translation machinery

candidate_datasets.name: Genome Taxonomy Database
candidate_datasets.role: standardized bacterial and archaeal genome phylogenies

obstacles: The earliest signal is obscured by horizontal gene transfer and sequence saturation.
All organisms that ever lived cannot be sampled directly.
rationale: Universal ancestry has explicit comparative-genomic predictions and massive public datasets. Exact singularity at life's origin remains inferential, but alternatives can be meaningfully discriminated with existing data.

operationalization: Measure genetic and phenotypic continuity within named varieties and species, including fossil or phylogenetic evidence for lost intermediates, and test whether discontinuity alone distinguishes the categories. Continuity gradients would support the empirical portion, but cannot establish that the distinction is only one of convenience.
obstacles: Species and variety are partly conventional categories with multiple concepts.
Former intermediates are absent by definition and often unpreserved.
Reproductive isolation provides distinctions beyond observed intermediates.
rationale: Continuity and divergence can be quantified for many groups. The exclusive, conceptual claim about the only distinction and classificatory convenience is not fully empirically resolvable.

operationalization: Partition trait change, diversification and extinction rates among models driven by biotic interactions versus physical environmental change across replicated fossil clades and modern radiations. Greater standardized explanatory contribution from biotic variables would support the comparative 'most important' claim.
obstacles: Biotic interactions are poorly preserved and incompletely recorded.
Biotic and physical drivers covary and operate at different scales.
Global causal importance has no single natural metric.
rationale: Existing data permit comparative tests in selected systems. The all-organism, all-time ranking of causes is underdetermined because interaction histories are sparse and confounded.

operationalization: For independently radiometrically dated formation pairs, quantify fossil assemblage turnover or phylogenetic change and test its relationship with elapsed time, then use held-out intervals to assess dating error. A stable monotonic calibrated relationship supports the claim.
obstacles: Turnover rates vary among clades and mass extinctions.
Sampling and preservation differ among formations.
Circular biostratigraphic age assignments must be excluded.
rationale: Independent numerical ages and fossil assemblages allow direct calibration and out-of-sample validation. Known rate heterogeneity makes the measure imperfect, exactly as the claim allows.

operationalization: Estimate rates of phenotypic and taxonomic change per unit time in early versus later fossil intervals, correcting for sampling, and compare rates with reconstructed diversity and complexity. Lower early rates would support the claim.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: fossil diversity and turnover through the Phanerozoic

candidate_datasets.name: Macrostrat
candidate_datasets.role: rock availability, stratigraphic context and ages

obstacles: The earliest history of life has an exceptionally sparse and biased record.
Molecular and morphological rate estimates are not directly comparable.
Complexity and rate of organic change have competing definitions.
rationale: Phanerozoic portions can be analyzed with existing data. The first dawn of life, which is central to the strongest prediction, lacks adequate temporal and organismal resolution.

operationalization: Compare the independently estimated age of life's first origin with the duration and completeness of the preserved geological record known to contain life. The claim requires the unrecorded pre-geological interval to greatly exceed the preserved interval.

candidate_datasets.name: Macrostrat
candidate_datasets.role: temporal coverage of preserved sedimentary geology

candidate_datasets.name: EarthChem
candidate_datasets.role: geochemical age and early-Earth evidence relevant to earliest life

obstacles: The time of the first organism is unknown and may predate surviving rocks.
The phrase 'known geological history' changes with discovery.
No possible fossil sample can directly cover destroyed Hadean crust.
rationale: The comparison is conceptually measurable, but its decisive endpoint—the first organism—is not present in current datasets. Existing geochemical constraints do not establish that the missing duration is larger than all known geological history.

operationalization: For prespecified cognitive capacities, map standardized behavioral and neural traits onto phylogenies and test whether complex states arise through ordered intermediate states rather than abrupt transitions. Repeated graded sequences support the claim for those capacities.

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Traits Database
candidate_datasets.role: comparative animal trait records, including behavioral traits

obstacles: Mental powers are heterogeneous and difficult to compare across species.
Ancestral cognition does not fossilize directly.
Phylogenetic gradualism can be mimicked by coarse trait coding.
rationale: Some cognitive traits admit comparative tests, but 'each mental power' is too broad and requires substantial interpretation. Current open data are sparse and biased toward a few taxa.

operationalization: In fossil intervals, treat species present at an earlier time as the prediction cohort and test whether initially common, widespread species in species-rich clades disproportionately persist or give rise to later diversity. Low descendant survival overall and positive effects of abundance, range and clade dominance support the claim.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: fossil abundance proxies, range, persistence and descendant diversity

candidate_datasets.name: Neotoma Paleoecology Database
candidate_datasets.role: high-resolution late-Quaternary occurrence and abundance records

obstacles: Direct ancestor-descendant links are rarely known.
Observed abundance and range are highly sampling-dependent.
The far future of living species is not directly testable.
rationale: Retrospective fossil cohorts can test close analogues of the prediction. They cannot literally resolve the future fate of present species, and genealogical descent is often uncertain.

operationalization: Test genomes of all major living lineages for uninterrupted genealogical continuity from deep ancestors and examine global stratigraphic and extinction records for an interval that eliminated all life. Any independently originated post-cataclysm lineage or truly sterile global break refutes the claim.

candidate_datasets.name: Macrostrat
candidate_datasets.role: global stratigraphic coverage and boundary context

obstacles: Absence of fossils cannot prove absence of survivors.
Microbial survival is poorly represented in occurrence databases.
Pre-Silurian ancestry is inferred from phylogeny rather than direct continuous fossils.
rationale: A worldwide sterilizing cataclysm and broken descent have strong genomic and geological consequences. Existing evidence spans all major lineages and extinction boundaries, though absolute proof of uninterrupted survival is limited by preservation.

operationalization: No non-arbitrary dataset test exists until 'good,' 'endowment' and 'perfection' are replaced by specified fitness components and environments. Such a replacement would test local adaptation, not the teleological claim as stated.
obstacles: Perfection has no environment-independent measurable endpoint.
Trade-offs allow the same change to count as improvement and deterioration.
Natural selection does not imply monotonic progress in every trait.
rationale: Public fitness and trait datasets are abundant, but they cannot adjudicate an undefined universal tendency toward perfection. Any operationalization would materially narrow and alter Darwin's statement.

operationalization: Fit integrated evolutionary models linking reproduction, inheritance, environmental and use-related variation, population growth, competition, selection, trait divergence and extinction to observed phylogenomic and fossil patterns. Compare predictive performance with models omitting each proposed process.

candidate_datasets.name: Global Biotic Interactions
candidate_datasets.role: ecological interactions relevant to struggle and selection

obstacles: No single dataset jointly observes all processes over evolutionary time.
Several listed mechanisms produce overlapping macroevolutionary signatures.
Inherited effects of use and disuse require historical reinterpretation.
rationale: Every component has measurable consequences and substantial public data, but the full causal synthesis cannot be cleanly identified from one integrated record. Existing analyses can resolve subsets and compare restricted process models.
